reason: Radioactive heating should change the interiors of the rocky planetesimals, helping expose their stone and metal.
expectation: The rocky bodies heat internally, potentially allowing metal and rock to separate.

alternatives.reason: Heating icy bodies may also advance the water-bearing rock goal.

effect: The rocky planetesimal has melted, making separation of its materials plausible.
reaction: The distinction that not all asteroids melt is useful.
reason: Gravity can drive dense metal inward in a molten body, separating it from rock.
expectation: The body will differentiate into metal-rich and rocky regions.

alternatives.reason: Collisions might expose material, but separation likely comes first.

effect: Metal and silicate have separated; the rocky layers need to cool before collisions can expose fragments.
reaction: The cooling requirement makes the sequence clear.
reason: Escaping radiation should cool and solidify the layered body.
expectation: The planetesimal cools, leaving solid rocky layers around its metal-rich interior.

effect: The asteroid has cooled and solidified, so collisions can now expose its differentiated materials.
reaction: The sequence from melting to solidification is clear.
reason: Collisions can break the cooled asteroid and expose its rocky and metal-rich layers.
expectation: The collision produces exposed stone and metal fragments.

effect: The collision produced rocky-layer fragments and completed the stone-and-metal goal; the remaining goal concerns water in altered rock.
reaction: The goal completion also accounts for metal, though this result specifically describes rocky fragments.
reason: Heating icy planetesimals may melt their ice and allow water to alter rock.
expectation: The icy bodies warm internally, potentially producing liquid water that can react with rock.

effect: Internal heating produced liquid water inside the icy body, making water–rock reactions possible.
reaction: The contrast between a frozen exterior and liquid water inside is interesting.
reason: Silicate grains provide rock for the liquid water to alter.

choice.combine: Liquid water inside an icy body

expectation: Water reacts with silicate rock, producing water-bearing altered minerals.

effect: The water reacted with silicates to form hydrated rock, completing the remaining goal and showing how hydrogen can be carried even after exposed ice disappears.
reaction: That connection between water–rock reactions and Earth's volatile inventory was interesting.

mostWorthwhile.text: Heating the icy body and reacting its liquid water with silicates was most worthwhile: it showed a plausible way water-derived hydrogen can be retained in rock.

leastWorthwhile.text: The collision result was somewhat confusing: it described rocky fragments while completing a goal that also mentioned exposed metal.

surprise.text: A frozen-looking body can contain liquid water, and its rock can retain hydrogen after exposed ice is gone.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though the metal part of the collision goal was not explicit in the result.

continue.text: Yes. I would be curious to see how these differentiated and water-bearing bodies contribute to a growing Earth; the physical explanations made their formation engaging.
